slides.title: Allocating memory that never runs out unexpectedly
points: On a device with kilobytes of RAM that runs for years, general-purpose malloc and free can fragment memory until an allocation fails.
Memory pools avoid that with fixed-size blocks.

slides.title: Fixed blocks, known limits
points: Fragmentation: free memory exists but in pieces too small for the request.
A pool pre-allocates N blocks of one size; allocation and free are fast and can't fragment.
Static allocation at start-up (no heap afterwards) makes worst-case memory use known at build time.
Track pool high-water marks to size pools correctly.

slides.title: Predictable against flexible
points: Pools waste space when objects are smaller than the block.
Several pools of different sizes cover varied needs.
A pool that runs out still needs a defined behaviour (reject, drop the oldest).

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: RTOS memory pools or a project's own block allocator.
Rules that forbid malloc after initialisation.
Long-running soak tests watching free memory.

slides.title: Recovering, and knowing why
points: A watchdog timer resets the device if the software stops checking in, so a hang doesn't last forever.
Field diagnostics record what happened, so failures in customers' hands can be understood.

slides.title: Kick correctly, record failures
points: Kick the watchdog only when the whole system is healthy (every critical task has reported), not from a timer interrupt that runs regardless.
Record the reset reason (watchdog, brown-out, crash) in memory that survives the reset.
Crash dumps: save the program counter, stack and a small log before resetting.
Upload diagnostics when the device next connects.

slides.title: Resetting hides bugs
points: A watchdog that silently resets makes devices look fine while bugs persist; count and report resets.
Diagnostics use flash and bandwidth; keep them compact.
Too short a timeout resets during legitimate slow operations.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Reset counters per cause in device telemetry.
Crash reports grouped by firmware version.
The watchdog tested deliberately before shipping.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Updating without bricking
points: Over-the-air (OTA) updates fix bugs and add features on devices already in the field.
A failed update must never leave the device unusable.

slides.title: Two slots, verify, roll back
points: A/B slots: write the new image to the inactive slot while the old one keeps running.
Verify the image's signature and integrity before switching.
Boot the new image on trial; if it doesn't confirm it's healthy, the bootloader rolls back.
Power can fail at any moment; every step must survive it.

slides.title: Flash space for safety
points: Two slots need twice the flash; compressed or delta updates reduce size and add complexity.
Unsigned updates let anyone install firmware; signing needs key management.
Staged rollouts catch bad releases before every device takes them.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: MCUboot or a vendor bootloader with signature checks.
Rollouts to a small fleet first, watching reset and crash rates.
Anti-rollback counters to stop downgrades to vulnerable versions.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Linux on devices
points: Larger embedded systems (routers, cameras, cars) run Linux, with drivers that connect the kernel to the hardware.
It brings networking, file systems and tools, and its own complexity.

slides.title: Kernel space, device tree, drivers
points: The kernel runs with full privileges; user programs talk to it through system calls and device files.
The device tree describes the board's hardware so one kernel can run on many boards.
A driver registers for a device, handles its interrupts and exposes it to user space.
Build systems (Yocto, Buildroot) assemble the kernel, bootloader and root file system.

slides.title: Capability against footprint
points: Linux needs megabytes of RAM and storage and seconds to boot.
It isn't hard real-time by default; real-time patches or a separate microcontroller handle tight timing.
Kernel bugs crash everything; prefer user-space drivers where they're fast enough.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: dmesg for kernel messages; /sys and /proc to inspect hardware and processes.
Upstream drivers preferred over vendor forks.
Security updates for the kernel planned for the device's lifetime.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Measuring where the time goes
points: Embedded performance is about meeting deadlines and saving power with limited CPU.
Profiling finds the real hot spots; guessing usually finds the wrong ones.

slides.title: Measure first
points: Toggle a GPIO at the start and end of a function and watch it on a scope: exact timing, nearly free.
Cycle counters (like the DWT counter on Cortex-M) time code precisely.
Sampling profilers and trace tools show where the CPU spends its time.
Optimise the measured hot spot: better algorithms, DMA, fixed-point maths, avoiding copies.

slides.title: Fast against readable
points: Hand-optimised code is harder to maintain; optimise only what measurements justify.
Compiler optimisation levels change timing and can hide or reveal bugs.
Measuring adds overhead; keep instrumentation light.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Timing budgets per task, checked in tests.
Logic analysers and oscilloscopes on the bench.
Profiles compared before and after each optimisation.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: When the bug might be in the hardware
points: Embedded bugs live in software, hardware, or the gap between them.
Hardware debugging tools let you see both.

slides.title: Probe, observe, isolate
points: A debug probe (JTAG/SWD) lets you halt the CPU, step code, read memory and set breakpoints.
An oscilloscope shows voltages over time: noise, slow edges, brown-outs.
A logic analyser decodes buses (I2C, SPI, UART) to show what was actually sent.
Isolate: known-good board, minimal firmware, one change at a time.

slides.title: Tools and patience
points: Breakpoints change timing; some bugs disappear when observed (use trace instead).
Probes and scopes cost money and bench time; they pay for themselves quickly.
Blaming hardware too early wastes time; so does blaming software.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Test points on boards for probing.
A bring-up checklist for new boards: power rails, clocks, debug link, then peripherals.
Notes of every measurement during an investigation.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: C on a whiteboard
points: Embedded interviews often ask for C: bit manipulation, pointer handling, a ring buffer, a simple driver.
They're checking for correctness with memory, types and edge cases.

slides.title: Common asks
points: Set, clear, toggle and test bits with masks and shifts.
Implement a ring buffer safely, including full and empty conditions.
Explain volatile, const, static and integer promotion.
Reason about endianness, alignment and structure padding.

slides.title: Clear and safe
points: Clever one-liners with undefined behaviour cost more than plain code.
Say the assumptions: integer sizes, interrupt context, concurrency.
Test by hand on edge cases: zero, full, wrap-around.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Write a ring buffer, a bit-field register driver and a fixed-point function from scratch.
Practise explaining memory layout of a struct.
Review undefined behaviour cases in C.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: 'The device resets randomly. What do you do?'
points: Interviewers describe a field failure and ask how you'd find the cause.
They're scoring method across software and hardware.

slides.title: Narrow it down
points: Gather facts: how often, which units, since which firmware, under what conditions.
Read the reset reason and any crash dump.
Form hypotheses (stack overflow, watchdog, brown-out, memory corruption) and test the cheapest first.
Reproduce on the bench, then fix and verify.

slides.title: Evidence over hunches
points: Guessing a favourite cause wastes time.
Fixes without reproduction are hopes.
Say when you'd involve hardware engineers.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Have a real debugging story with your steps.
Know the usual causes of random resets and how to tell them apart.
Talk through tools: debugger, scope, logs.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Design the software for a product
points: You're asked to design firmware for a device: a smart thermostat, a fitness band, an industrial sensor.
They're scoring architecture, constraints and reliability thinking.

slides.title: Cover the essentials
points: Requirements and constraints: power budget, memory, connectivity, safety.
Architecture: tasks or a state machine, drivers, communication, storage.
Reliability: watchdog, error handling, safe updates, diagnostics.
Testing: unit tests on host, hardware-in-the-loop, field telemetry.

slides.title: Say the costs
points: An RTOS versus bare metal: justify it.
Battery life against responsiveness and features.
Security of updates and communication from the start.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Practise two designs end to end on paper.
Draw the task diagram and the update flow.
Mention how you'd test without the hardware.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: A device crashes after about three weeks of uptime with an allocation failure, though total free heap is still large. What's happening?
choices: Fragmentation: free memory is split into small pieces; use fixed-size pools or allocate everything at start-up
why: Plenty free in total but no single piece big enough is the signature of fragmentation.
Possible in other bugs, but not this symptom.

newQuestions.stem: The watchdog is kicked from a 1 ms timer interrupt. A task deadlocks, but the device never resets. Why?
choices: The timer interrupt keeps kicking it regardless of the tasks' health; kick only after every critical task has checked in
why: A watchdog must prove the system is alive, not just that one interrupt runs.

newQuestions.stem: During an OTA update, power is lost halfway through writing. Which design keeps the device working?
choices: A/B slots: the update writes to the inactive slot, so the old firmware still boots
Write over the running firmware quickly
Ask users not to unplug devices
why: The running image is never touched until the new one is complete and verified.

newQuestions.stem: A new sensor on an embedded Linux board isn't detected, though its driver is built into the kernel. What should you check first?
choices: The device tree: is the sensor described with the right bus, address and compatible string?
why: Drivers bind to devices the device tree declares.

newQuestions.stem: A control loop misses its 1 ms deadline. Someone wants to rewrite the maths in assembly. What first?
choices: Measure where the time goes (GPIO toggles or cycle counters), then optimise the actual hot spot
why: Without measurement, effort goes to the wrong place.
Expensive and maybe not where the time goes.
May help but costs power and redesign.

newQuestions.stem: An I2C sensor returns wrong values occasionally. The code looks correct. What's a good next step?
choices: Capture the bus with a logic analyser (and check signal edges with a scope) to see what's really transmitted
why: Seeing the real traffic separates software bugs from signal problems.
Without evidence, a rewrite may keep the bug.

newQuestions.stem: Which expression clears bit 3 of `reg` and leaves the others unchanged?
why: AND with the inverted mask clears exactly that bit.

newQuestions.stem: Units in the field reset when a motor starts. What's a strong first hypothesis to check?
choices: A brown-out: the motor's current draw dips the supply voltage; check the reset reason and the rail on a scope
A bug in the display code
why: The timing points at power; the reset cause and a scope confirm it.
Possible, but timing points to power.

newQuestions.stem: Designing firmware for a battery-powered sensor that reports every 10 minutes, what drives most decisions?
choices: The power budget: sleep most of the time, wake on a timer, measure and send in one short burst
why: Battery life dominates; duty cycling decides the architecture.
